40035:
1 Kings opens with an old, cold David and a palace power struggle. Adonijah makes himself king, but Nathan and Bathsheba secure the throne for Solomon (1 Kgs 1). Solomon consolidates power, asks God for wisdom rather than riches, and builds the temple and his palace with Phoenician help. His reign is pictured as a golden age: peace, trade, international fame and wisdom 'that excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east country' (1 Kgs 4:30).

Archaeologists debate how grand Solomon's kingdom really was. Yigael Yadin linked similar six-chambered gates at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer to Solomon's building projects (1 Kgs 9:15). Israel Finkelstein's 'low chronology' redates many of these structures to the 9th century and the Omride kings, picturing 10th-century Jerusalem as modest. Others (Amihai Mazar, Yosef Garfinkel) argue for a significant 10th-century state. The question remains open.

The narrator shows cracks in the golden age. Solomon takes 700 wives and 300 concubines, many from nations Israel was told not to marry, and builds shrines for their gods (1 Kgs 11:1-8). He also uses forced labour and heavy taxes. When his son Rehoboam refuses to lighten the load, the ten northern tribes break away under Jeroboam (1 Kgs 12). Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan so that his people will not go to Jerusalem (1 Kgs 12:26-30), a sin the narrator holds against every later northern king.

The second half focuses on the northern kingdom under the Omride dynasty, especially Ahab and his Phoenician queen Jezebel, who promote the worship of Baal. Into this crisis steps Elijah the Tishbite. He announces drought (a direct challenge to Baal, the storm god), confronts the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and, when Jezebel threatens him, flees to Horeb, where God meets him not in wind, earthquake or fire, but in 'a still small voice' (1 Kgs 19:12). Kings presents prophets as the covenant's enforcers, calling kings back to the LORD.
40037: Ancient temples were seen as divine palaces. Solomon's temple followed a common Syro-Phoenician layout (porch, main hall, inner sanctuary), similar to the temple excavated at Ain Dara in Syria. But no statue of God stood inside.

Kings is the last of the Former Prophets in the Hebrew Bible, and many of its chapters are read as haftarot. When the Torah tells of Abraham's old age (Gen 23-25), the haftarah is David's old age and Solomon's succession (1 Kgs 1:1-31). When Jacob blesses his sons on his deathbed, the haftarah is David's charge to Solomon (1 Kgs 2:1-12). The building of the temple is read with the building of the tabernacle (1 Kgs 5:12-6:13), and Elijah on Mount Carmel (1 Kgs 18) is read with the golden calf (Exod 30-34), two stories about Israel wavering between God and an idol. Solomon's dedication prayer (1 Kgs 8) is read on Sukkot, since the dedication took place at that feast (1 Kgs 8:2).

Elijah holds a unique place in Jewish life. Because he was taken up alive (2 Kgs 2:11) and Malachi promises he will return before the day of the LORD (Mal 4:5-6), Jewish tradition sees him as the forerunner of the Messiah. A cup is poured for Elijah at the Passover Seder and the door opened for him; a chair is set for him at every circumcision; and the song *Eliyahu ha-Navi* is sung at the close of every Sabbath. The rabbis say Elijah will settle unresolved questions of law (the word *teku*, 'let it stand', was later read as an acronym pointing to him).

Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication is the heart of the book for its first audience. He admits that 'the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee' (1 Kgs 8:27) and asks that when Israel sins and is taken captive to a far land, if they pray toward this house and repent, God will hear and forgive (1 Kgs 8:46-50). Exiles in Babylon prayed toward Jerusalem on the basis of this prayer (compare Dan 6:10), and Jews still face Jerusalem when they pray. The covenant relationship did not end with the temple's destruction; Solomon himself had made provision for repentance in exile.

40126:
2 Kings covers about three centuries in which the small kingdoms of Israel and Judah were caught between superpowers. In the 9th century the threat came from Aram (Damascus), whose kings fought Israel for decades. From the mid-8th century the Neo-Assyrian Empire under Tiglath-pileser III began a new policy: conquering, deporting and resettling whole populations to break national identities. The northern kingdom of Israel, weakened by coups (four kings were assassinated in about fifteen years, 2 Kgs 15), was swallowed up. Samaria fell in 722 BC, its people were deported and foreigners settled in their place (2 Kgs 17:6; 2 Kgs 17:24).

Judah survived another 135 years. Hezekiah reformed worship, built the Siloam tunnel to bring water inside Jerusalem (2 Kgs 20:20; its Hebrew inscription was found in 1880), and resisted Sennacherib in 701 BC. Assyria's own annals boast of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem but do not claim to have taken it, which fits the Bible's account of the city's deliverance (2 Kgs 19:35-36). But Hezekiah's son Manasseh reigned 55 years and filled Judah with idolatry and violence (2 Kgs 21:1-16), and the narrator marks this as the point of no return.

Josiah, the last great reformer, purged idolatry after the book of the law was found in the temple (2 Kgs 22-23). He is praised above all kings (2 Kgs 23:25), yet he died at Megiddo fighting Pharaoh Neco (2 Kgs 23:29). After him, Judah lurched between Egypt and Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem in 597 BC, deporting King Jehoiachin, the elite and craftsmen (including the young Ezekiel). When Zedekiah rebelled, Babylon returned, burned the temple in 586 BC and deported most of the rest.

Against this backdrop stand the prophets. Elisha, Elijah's successor, performs more miracles than anyone in the Old Testament: healing water, multiplying oil and bread, raising a dead boy, healing the Syrian general Naaman. Kings also names Jonah (2 Kgs 14:25) and Isaiah (2 Kgs 19-20) and the prophetess Huldah (2 Kgs 22:14). The narrator's verdict on the north is explicit: the LORD 'testified against Israel... by all the prophets', but they would not hear (2 Kgs 17:13-14).
40128: Assyria moved conquered peoples across the empire to prevent revolt. The resettled people in Samaria mixed their gods with worship of the LORD, the background to the later Samaritans.
40130: Small kings paid annual tribute to stay alive. Stopping payment meant rebellion, and Kings shows Hoshea, Hezekiah, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah taking that gamble.

40139:
The Elisha stories are favourites in the synagogue haftarah cycle. The Shunammite woman promised a son (2 Kgs 4:1-37) is read with the story of Sarah promised Isaac (Gen 18); Naaman's healing (2 Kgs 5) with the laws of skin disease (Lev 12-13); and the four lepers who discover the abandoned Aramean camp (2 Kgs 7:3-20) with the laws of purification (Lev 14-15). Josiah's great Passover (2 Kgs 23) is read on the second day of Passover, and the account of Jehoash repairing the temple with public funds (2 Kgs 12) is read on Shabbat Shekalim, when the annual half-shekel for the temple was announced.

The rabbis drew moral lessons from the kings. Hezekiah is praised for spreading Torah study so widely that, according to the Talmud (Sanhedrin 94b), there was no child in the land unfamiliar with the laws of purity. Manasseh, the worst king, became a symbol of the power of repentance: Chronicles says he repented in captivity (2 Chr 33:12-13), and the rabbis debated whether even he has a share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2 lists him among those who do not, but other teachers say his repentance was accepted). Elijah's chariot of fire made him a living link between heaven and earth.

The first audience, exiles in Babylon, would have heard 2 Kings as a hard but honest confession. The narrator's long sermon at the fall of Samaria (2 Kgs 17:7-23) lists the sins: other gods, high places, ignoring the prophets, rejecting the covenant. Judah did the same. This was not God's failure but Israel's. Yet the book refuses to end in despair. Its last scene shows Jehoiachin, the exiled son of David, released from prison and given a seat at the king's table 'all the days of his life' (2 Kgs 25:29-30). The line of David survives. The covenant relationship, though wounded, is not dead, and readers are left to wait, like Solomon prayed, for God to hear from heaven and forgive (1 Kgs 8:46-50).
